n: About August 591 BC, elders again come to Ezekiel to ask the Lord a question. God responds with a review of Israel’s whole history of rebellion.

f.w: the seventh year, in the fifth month
f.g: About August 591 BC, counting from Jehoiachin’s exile.

f.w: came to inquire of the LORD

n: The Lord speaks to Ezekiel.

f.w: Then came the word of the LORD unto me
f.g: God answers the elders’ visit.

n: God refuses to be consulted by them. As in chapter 14, people still clinging to idols are not in a position to receive revelation.

f.w: I will not be inquired of by you

n: Instead of an oracle, Ezekiel is to “judge” them—confront them with the sins of their ancestors.

f.w: Wilt thou judge them
f.g: Bring an indictment against them.

n: It began in Egypt: God chose Israel, swore an oath to them (raising his hand), and revealed himself: “I am the LORD your God.”

f.w: lifted up mine hand
f.g: A gesture of swearing an oath.

f.w: made myself known unto them

n: He swore to bring them to a land he had scouted for them—flowing with milk and honey, the most beautiful of lands.

f.w: flowing with milk and honey
espied
f.g: Searched out, scouted.

n: God commanded them to throw away the idols of Egypt they loved to look at.

f.w: the abominations of his eyes
f.g: Idols they found attractive.

f.w: the idols of Egypt

n: But they rebelled and kept their Egyptian idols. God was ready to pour out his anger even in Egypt.

f.w: neither did they forsake the idols of Egypt
f.g: This detail is not recorded in Exodus but fits Israel’s later behavior (the golden calf).

n: Yet God acted “for his name’s sake”—to protect his reputation before the nations who saw him deliver Israel. This phrase is the refrain of the chapter.

f.w: I wrought for my name's sake

n: So he brought them out of Egypt into the wilderness.

f.w: brought them into the wilderness

n: He gave them laws that bring life to those who live by them.

f.w: which if a man do, he shall even live in them

n: He also gave them his Sabbaths as a sign that it is the Lord who makes them holy. Sabbath-keeping was a mark of covenant identity.

f.w: my sabbaths, to be a sign between me and them

n: Israel rebelled in the wilderness too, despising God’s laws and profaning his Sabbaths. God considered destroying them there.

f.w: rebelled against me in the wilderness

n: Again he spared them for his name’s sake.

f.w: that it should not be polluted before the heathen
f.g: So that his name would not be dishonored among the nations.

n: Still, God swore that the rebellious generation would not enter the promised land.

f.w: that I would not bring them into the land

n: This was because their hearts kept going after idols.

f.w: their heart went after their idols

n: Even so, God looked on them with pity and did not wipe them out.

f.w: mine eye spared them

n: He warned their children in the wilderness not to follow their parents’ ways or their idols. Each generation gets a fresh chance, as in chapter 18.

f.w: Walk ye not in the statutes of your fathers

n: “I am the LORD your God; walk in my statutes.”

f.w: walk in my statutes

n: Keep my Sabbaths holy as a sign of our relationship.

f.w: hallow
f.g: Keep holy.

n: But the children also rebelled, and God again was ready to pour out his anger.

f.w: the children rebelled against me

n: Once more he held back his hand for the sake of his name.

f.w: I withdrew mine hand
f.g: Restrained his judgment.

n: Even in the wilderness God warned through Moses that persistent rebellion would end in scattering among the nations.

f.w: I would scatter them among the heathen

n: That scattering was the consequence of rejecting his laws and longing for their fathers’ idols.

f.w: their eyes were after their fathers' idols
f.g: Their desires stayed fixed on idols.

n: A difficult verse: God “gave them” laws that were not good. It likely means he let them follow the destructive pagan customs they chose—handing them over to their own choices as judgment.

f.w: statutes that were not good
f.g: Probably the corrupt practices they adopted, which God allowed as a consequence.

n: He let them defile themselves through their offerings—even sacrificing their firstborn children in fire—so that the horror would bring them to recognize the Lord.

f.w: caused to pass through the fire all that openeth the womb
f.g: Child sacrifice to Molech, a perversion of the law that the firstborn belonged to God.

n: After entering the land, their ancestors blasphemed God by being unfaithful.

f.w: blasphemed
f.g: Insulted, dishonored.

n: Once in Canaan they offered sacrifices on every high hill and under every leafy tree—offerings that provoked God.

f.w: every high hill, and all the thick trees
drink offerings
f.g: Wine poured out as an offering.

n: A sarcastic wordplay: “What is this high place (bamah) you go (ba’im) to?” The name stuck—they still called such places “Bamah.”

f.w: Bamah
f.g: Hebrew for “high place.” The pun mocks the shrines.

n: Now God turns to the present generation: are you defiling yourselves just like your fathers?

f.w: Are ye polluted after the manner of your fathers?
f.g: The history lesson is aimed at the elders in front of Ezekiel.

n: Since they still make their sons pass through fire and worship idols, God will not let them consult him.

f.w: I will not be inquired of by you

n: Some thought, “Let’s just be like the other nations and worship wood and stone.” God says that will never happen; he won’t let his people simply disappear into paganism.

f.w: We will be as the heathen

n: God swears he will rule over them with a mighty hand and outstretched arm—the same power he used to free them from Egypt.

f.w: with a mighty hand, and with a stretched out arm

n: He will gather them out of the nations where they are scattered. A new exodus is promised.

f.w: will gather you out of the countries

n: He will bring them into “the wilderness of the peoples” and there judge them face to face, as he did at Sinai.

f.w: the wilderness of the people
f.g: The lands of exile, pictured as a new wilderness journey.

f.w: face to face

n: As he judged their ancestors in the wilderness of Egypt, so he will judge them.

f.w: Like as I pleaded with your fathers

n: Like a shepherd counting sheep as they pass under his staff, God will examine each person and bring them into the covenant bond.

f.w: pass under the rod
f.g: Shepherds counted and inspected sheep as they passed under a rod.

f.w: the bond of the covenant

n: He will separate out the rebels; they will not enter the land of Israel—just as the rebellious wilderness generation did not.

f.w: I will purge out from among you the rebels

n: With bitter irony God says: go ahead and serve your idols if you won’t listen—but stop profaning my holy name by mixing them with my worship.

f.w: pollute ye my holy name no more

n: On God’s holy mountain, all Israel will one day serve him, and he will accept their offerings again—a promise of restored temple worship.

f.w: in mine holy mountain
oblations
f.g: Offerings.

n: When he gathers them, he will accept them as a pleasing offering and show his holiness through them before the nations.

f.w: I will be sanctified in you before the heathen

n: Brought back to the land promised to their fathers, they will know he is the Lord.

f.w: I lifted up mine hand to give it to your fathers

n: There they will remember their past and feel deep sorrow for it. True repentance often comes most fully after experiencing God’s mercy.

f.w: ye shall lothe yourselves

n: They will know the Lord when they see that he dealt with them for his name’s sake—graciously—rather than as their sins deserved.

f.w: not according to your wicked ways

n: A new short oracle begins. (In the Hebrew Bible, verses 45–49 begin chapter 21.)

f.w: Moreover the word of the LORD came unto me
f.g: Hebrew Bibles number 20:45-49 as 21:1-5.

n: Ezekiel turns toward the south—Judah, which lay south of the route Babylon’s armies would take—and prophesies against its “forest.”

f.w: the south
f.g: Three different Hebrew words for “south” are used here, perhaps hinting at Judah and the Negev.

f.w: drop thy word
f.g: Let your words flow, preach.

n: God will light an unquenchable fire that burns every tree, green and dry, from south to north. Chapter 21 shows the fire is Babylon’s sword.

f.w: every green tree in thee, and every dry tree

n: Everyone will see that the Lord kindled this fire, and it won’t be put out.

f.w: it shall not be quenched

n: Ezekiel complains: people dismiss him as just “a teller of parables.” His vivid stories were being treated as entertainment rather than warning—so in chapter 21 God speaks plainly.

f.w: Doth he not speak parables?
